fetched_contents.text: Short-term Detection of Fast Progressors in Glaucoma: The Fast-PACE (Progression Assessment through Clustered Evaluation) Study . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2025 Jul 29. Published in final edited form as: Ophthalmology. 2023 Dec 29;131(6):645–657. doi: 10.1016/j.ophtha.2023.12.031 Abstract Purpose: To evaluate the performance of an intensive, clustered testing approach in identifying eyes with rapid glaucoma progression over 6 months in the Fast-PACE (Progression Assessment through Clustered Evaluation) study. Design: Prospective cohort study. Participants: 125 eyes from 65 primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) subjects. Methods: Subjects underwent two sets of 5 weekly visits (clusters) separated by an average of 6 months, then were followed with single visits every 6 months for an overall mean follow-up of 25 months (mean of 17 tests). Each visit consisted of testing with standard automated perimetry (SAP) 24–2 and 10–2, and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD OCT). Progression was assessed using trend analyses of SAP mean deviation (MD) and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness. Generalized estimating equations were applied to adjust for correlations between eyes for confidence interval (CI) estimation and hypothesis testing. Main Outcome Measures: Diagnostic accuracy of the 6-month clustering period to identify progression detected during the overall follow-up. Results: 19 of 125 eyes (15%, CI: 9%−24%) progressed based on SAP 24-2 MD over the 6-month clustering period. 14 eyes (11%, CI: 6%−20%) progressed on SAP 10–2 MD, and 16 (13%, CI:8%−21%) by RNFL thickness, with 30 of 125 eyes (24%, CI:16%−34%) progressing by function, structure, or both. Of the 35 eyes progressing during the overall follow-up, 25 had progressed during the 6-month clustering period, for a sensitivity of 71% (CI: 53%−85%). Of the 90 eyes that did not progress during the overall follow-up, 85 also did not progress during the 6-month period, for a specificity of 94% (CI: 88% – 98%). Of the 14 eyes considered fast progressors by SAP 24–2, 10–2 or SD OCT during the overall follow-up, 13 were identified as progressing during the 6-month cluster period, for a sensitivity of 93% (CI: 66% – 100%) for identifying fast progression with a specificity of 85% (CI: 77% – 90%). Conclusion: Clustered testing in the Fast-PACE study detected fast-progressing glaucoma eyes over six months. The methodology could be applied in clinical trials investigating interventions to slow glaucoma progression and may also be of value for short-term assessment of high-risk subjects. Reduction of intraocular pressure (IOP) has been shown to slow down disease progression, but some patients continue to progress despite well-controlled IOP.6,7 Neuroprotective therapies aimed at directly protecting neural tissue from damage via non-IOP mechanisms would likely be essential to prevent blindness in such cases. However, the development of such therapies has been hindered by difficulties in designing effective clinical trials to assess progression outcomes. Given that most patients progress slowly, it is generally believed that glaucoma trials require large sample sizes or very long follow-up periods to identify differential rates of disease worsening between treatment groups.8 Identifying fast progressors is further complicated by test-retest variability of the commonly available clinical tools, such as standard automated perimetry (SAP) and optical coherence tomography (OCT). Many strategies have been proposed to improve the efficacy of detecting progression in glaucoma. Clustering tests at both ends of the observation period – that is, having multiple measurements at the start and end of the period – has been proposed as a strategy to improve the efficacy of statistical tests to assess progression using trend-based analyses of test measurements over time.9,10 This approach can more accurately estimate the starting and ending points of the linear regression line, which can improve detection of significant changes over time. Using simulated data, Crabb and colleagues10 proposed the “wait and see” approach by which clustering tests at the start and end of the observation period would lead to better detection of fast progressors. Other simulation studies have also shown the potential of clustered testing to reduce sample sizes in clinical trials.11,12 In addition to their potential for leading to more efficient trials, a clustered testing approach may prove beneficial for prompt evaluation of patients whose further progression could place them at high risk of visual disability, severely and irreversibly impacting their quality of life. fetched_contents.text: Modifying Your Glaucoma Regimen: When, Why and How As optometrists, we are well positioned to diagnose and treat glaucoma; however, it’s not as simple as identifying someone with elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and then lowering it as much as possible. One report from nearly 20 years ago calculated more than 56,000 ways to treat glaucoma after taking into account all available medications and possible regimens ranging from monotherapy to maximum medical therapy.1 With new treatments at our disposal, that number is now considerably higher. In addition, glaucoma itself is a complex condition with varying presentations, rates of progression and responses to treatment. Properly treating the condition first requires the clinician to accurately identify the type of glaucoma, order and analyze appropriate testing and initiate an appropriate treatment plan with suitable follow up—there is no one-size-fits-all treatment protocol. Although glaucoma care remains more of an art than an exact science, a structured approach allows us to initiate—and tweak—treatment plans for each individual. Where You Start Matters The diagnosis and decision to initiate treatment is based on a comprehensive glaucoma workup that includes a detailed case history, slit lamp biomicroscopy, tonometry, pachymetry, gonioscopy, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) and ganglion cell complex imaging, perimetry and dilated optic nerve assessment. One of the most challenging aspects of managing glaucoma is the interpretation of this conglomeration of data. The dilated fundus exam, with an assessment of the optic nerve head, is one of the most important parts of a glaucoma evaluation. Pay close attention to the cup-to-disc ratio, integrity of the neuroretinal rim and the presence or absence of an optic disc hemorrhage, peripapillary changes and baring or bayoneting of the retinal vasculature. Indications of glaucomatous changes noted during a dilated fundus exam should correlate and be consistent with optical coherence tomography (OCT) and visual field findings to warrant initiation of treatment. Beyond using gonioscopy for the initial diagnosis and classification of glaucoma, this testing should be repeated annually, as the anterior chamber angle tends to narrow with age. When determining whether to initiate treatment, pachymetry values and corneal hysteresis are especially important, as patients with thin corneas and low corneal hysteresis values are at an increased risk of developing glaucoma.2 Fig. 1. This 92-year-old white female is currently taking latanoprost OU at bedtime. She has a maximum IOP of 22mm Hg with an IOP on exam of 18mm Hg OU. Corneal thicknesses are 523µm OD and 520µm OS. The patient’s testing shows only mild visual field loss. Given her age and clinical picture, it is unlikely she will experience real functional impairment in her lifetime. A mild (even if confirmed) progression of RNFL loss might not be an indication to escalate therapy. Click images to enlarge. First-line Options The decision to initiate treatment—and what treatment to start with—should take into account testing, exam findings, the individual’s risk factors for developing glaucoma, the burden of long-term treatment, possible adverse effects, inconvenience and cost.3 Initial therapy with drops or selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) are both acceptable first-line treatments. Prostaglandin analogs have been the preferred initial pharmaceutical treatment due to their ability to effectively lower IOP with a once-daily dose.4 Research shows prostaglandin analogs are superior to other topical IOP-lowering classes in controlling diurnal and nocturnal IOP.4 Prostaglandins are also extremely safe, with no reported systemic adverse reactions.5 However, ocular side effects include darkening of iris color, lash growth, periocular skin pigmentation, fat distribution changes and conjunctival hyperemia.4,5 These ocular side effects should be considered, especially when treating unilaterally or in younger patients. SLT is also a viable first-line treatment option. Recently, the Laser in Glaucoma and Ocular Hypertension Study demonstrated that SLT is both clinically effective and cost-effective as an initial intervention for primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) and ocular hypertension.6 The benefits of SLT include eliminating the risk of poor compliance with medications, given the burdens placed on patients who must take one or more topical hypotensive agents daily. Change Tactics After initiating therapy, follow-up is guided by the severity of disease. Typically, monitoring patients with serial OCT and visual fields every six to 12 months for mild disease and every six months for moderate to severe disease is sufficient. The concept of reaching a target IOP has gained acceptance in glaucoma management; however, it remains unclear whether that target number should be a percent reduction, an absolute number, low IOP fluctuations or low nocturnal IOP.7 This treatment approach was reinforced by a post hoc analysis from the Advanced Glaucoma Intervention Study, which suggested that lowering IOP to below 18mm Hg at all visits or an average IOP of 12.3mm Hg would halt glaucoma progression.4 Other landmark glaucoma studies provide evidence for percent reduction in IOP. Still, practitioners who rigidly adhere to a target level or range may potentially be doing more harm than good, especially in low-risk patients with thick corneas.4 The target IOP concept is also limited by the fact that glaucoma care involves balancing the complex set of risks and benefits that accompany escalating therapy. Simply adding medications to reach a target IOP, regardless of evidence of disease progression, does not take these considerations into account. Current authoritative guidance on early glaucoma monitoring intervals

The evidence provided does not show an explicit AAO recommendation for shorter follow-up intervals as a blanket rule for early glaucoma. Instead, AAO’s summary benchmarks and related guidance emphasize individualized monitoring and the importance of follow-up being tailored to the patient’s needs, not just a fixed schedule [N1-F1]. The AAO’s Preferred Practice Pattern (PPP) for primary open-angle glaucoma explicitly states that follow-up should be guided by the patient’s response to therapy and that more frequent intervals may be needed after adjustments to therapy [N1-R2]. It also notes that follow-up should be considered more frequent in the context of perioperative care, such as within 6 weeks of surgery or sooner if optic-nerve-related damage is suspected [N1-R1]. However, these statements are context-specific and do not indicate a general shift to shorter intervals for all early glaucoma patients.

The standard current approach for early glaucoma, as reflected in the evidence, is a structured but flexible schedule. AAO guidance says that follow-up examinations should be “performed” at intervals appropriate to the patient’s condition and treatment response, with more frequent follow-up after therapy changes [N1-R2]. Practical clinical sources similarly describe a default of every 6–12 months for stable mild disease and recommend more frequent visits when disease severity, treatment response, or risk factors suggest that closer monitoring is needed [N5-F4]. In addition, the evidence notes that follow-up is usually guided by disease severity after therapy initiation, with monitoring usually every 6 to 12 months for mild disease and more frequent intervals for moderate to severe disease [N5-F4]. That means the “standard” for early glaucoma is not a single rigid interval but a baseline that may be adjusted upward.

For tests, the evidence is consistent that visual field testing is important for monitoring progression, and the recommendations are practical rather than excessively frequent. The evidence says that guidelines recommend at least annual testing, but that more frequent testing may be needed if there is evidence of change [N3-R1]. Another source says most patients have field testing once a year, and if a change is seen, the field is repeated within 1 to 3 months depending on likelihood of true change [N3-R3]. AAO’s explanation of visual field testing also notes that frequent testing helps detect progression early and that the frequency should be adjusted based on the patient’s condition [N3-R4]. For OCT and optic nerve imaging, the evidence states that monitoring with serial OCT and visual fields is usually sufficient for mild disease, with more frequent intervals for moderate to severe disease [N5-F4]. In other words, the core recommended tests are visual fields and OCT/imaging, and they are repeated at intervals that depend on disease severity and treatment response [N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-F4].

Overall, the current authoritative guidance is that early glaucoma follow-up is individualized: AAO emphasizes individualized monitoring and more frequent intervals after therapy changes [N1-F1][N1-R2], while practical sources support every 6–12 months for stable mild disease and more frequent visits when disease severity, treatment response, or risk factors suggest closer monitoring [N5-F4]. The tests recommended are visual field testing and serial OCT/imaging, with repetition guided by whether the patient is stable or showing signs of progression [N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-F4].

Evidence for when shorter intervals are appropriate and what factors support them

The evidence supports shorter intervals in early glaucoma mainly when there is evidence of progression, instability, or higher risk of rapid deterioration. A key study in the evidence shows that clustered testing over 6 months detected a substantial proportion of eyes with rapid glaucoma progression, with high sensitivity for identifying fast progressors [N2-F2]. This suggests that shorter, more intensive monitoring can be appropriate for patients whose disease may progress quickly, because conventional annual or even semiannual testing may miss rapid change. The same source also notes that clustered testing may be valuable for short-term assessment of high-risk subjects, especially because many patients progress slowly but some progress rapidly, putting them at high risk of visual disability [N2-F2].

Risk factors that justify more frequent monitoring are not listed exhaustively in the provided evidence, but several relevant factors are implied. The evidence indicates that patients with thin corneas, low corneal hysteresis, or other ocular risk factors are at increased risk of glaucoma and may need closer monitoring [N5-F4]. It also states that follow-up is guided by the severity of disease, treatment response, and patient-specific risk factors [N5-F4]. Additionally, the evidence highlights that follow-up may be more frequent after adjustments to therapy and that progressive optic nerve damage may require changes in therapy [N1-R2]. In practical clinical guidance, the evidence also notes that higher-risk or less stable cases require more frequent visits [N6-R4]. Taken together, these suggest that shorter intervals are appropriate for patients with unstable disease, treatment response, or known risk factors that raise the likelihood of progression [N2-F2][N5-F4][N6-R4].

Evidence for progression risk in early glaucoma is mixed but clearly present. The evidence notes that glaucoma is often considered to have a protracted course, but some progress rapidly and are at high risk for disability [N2-F2]. It also states that nearly two-thirds of untreated Chinese patients with normal-tension glaucoma progressed over an average follow-up of 70 months by visual field, RNFL, or ganglion cell inner plexiform layer measures [N2-R3]. That supports the idea that even in early glaucoma, progression can occur and may not be reliably predicted by a single normal visit. The evidence also emphasizes that detection of progression is important for effective management and that clustered testing can improve detection of fast progressors [N2-F2].

Clinical signs or test results that warrant adjusting intervals are explicitly mentioned in the evidence. The evidence says that follow-up should be more frequent after therapy adjustments and that progressive optic nerve damage despite achieving target IOP may require changes in therapy [N1-R2]. It also states that monitoring patients with serial OCT and visual fields every 6 to 12 months is usually sufficient for mild disease, but that more frequent intervals are needed for moderate to severe disease [N5-F4]. In addition, the evidence indicates that if a change is seen on visual field testing, the field should be repeated within 1 to 3 months depending on likelihood of true change [N3-R3]. So, signs of change on OCT, visual fields, or other structural/function tests, plus evidence of progression or treatment instability, are the main reasons to shorten intervals [N1-R2][N3-R3][N5-F4].

In summary, shorter intervals are appropriate when there is evidence of rapid progression, unstable disease, or higher-risk factors [N2-F2][N5-F4][N6-R4]. The evidence supports this with direct findings on fast progressors, plus practical guidance that follow-up is guided by disease severity, treatment response, and signs of progression [N2-F2][N5-F4]. The main factors that support shorter intervals are rapid progression risk, treatment instability, and abnormal test results indicating change or damage [N1-R2][N2-F2][N3-R3][N5-F4].

Practical comparison of the physician’s intervals with current practice

The physician’s recommended intervals—routine exams every 6–12 months, visual field tests, and optic nerve imaging if progression is suspected—are largely consistent with current authoritative guidance, but not identical. The AAO guidance emphasizes individualized monitoring and more frequent follow-up after therapy changes or perioperative concerns, rather than a single fixed schedule [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Practical clinical guidance similarly says that follow-up is usually guided by disease severity after therapy initiation, with monitoring usually every 6 to 12 months for mild disease and more frequent intervals for moderate to severe disease [N5-F4]. So the physician’s baseline of 6–12 months is not outdated in the sense of being invalid; it is the standard starting point for stable mild glaucoma, and the evidence supports keeping it unless risk factors or treatment response suggest closer monitoring [N1-F1][N5-F4].

The physician’s intervals are likely outdated in a narrower sense only when the patient has unstable disease, rapid progression risk, or other signs that justify shorter intervals. The evidence for shorter intervals is strongest when there is evidence of progression or rapid deterioration. A direct study shows that clustered testing over 6 months detected a substantial proportion of fast-progressing glaucoma eyes, with high sensitivity for identifying rapid progression [N2-F2]. That means the 6–12 month interval may miss fast progressors, and shorter, more frequent monitoring may be appropriate for those at high risk [N2-F2]. The evidence also indicates that follow-up may be more frequent after therapy adjustments and that progressive optic nerve damage may require changes in therapy [N1-R2]. In practical terms, the 6–12 month schedule is reasonable only for patients who are stable, have no signs of progression, and are responding well to treatment [N5-F4].

If everything is stable, every 6–12 months is fine [N5-F4]. But if the disease is unstable, treatment is changing, or there are signs of progression, more frequent visits are often needed [N1-R2][N2-F2]. The key is not that the older schedule is wrong, but that it is the baseline schedule, not the only schedule. If the patient is doing well and not showing change, the intervals are still reasonable; if there are red flags, the schedule may need to be adjusted [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Overall, the physician’s intervals are not outdated in general; they are the standard starting point for early glaucoma. They are likely outdated only if the patient has signs of progression, treatment instability, or high-risk factors that make shorter intervals more appropriate [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].

## Final answer: Are these intervals old? Updated explanation

### Short answer
The intervals your physician gave are **not outdated in general**. They are a **good starting point** for early glaucoma, and the evidence supports them as the standard for stable disease. But current guidance says follow-up should be **individualized**, which means the 6–12 month schedule is reasonable only if the patient is stable, not showing progression, and responding well to treatment. If the disease is unstable, treatment is changing, or there are signs of rapid progression, shorter intervals may be more appropriate.

## 1. What the current authoritative guidance says

The evidence provided does **not** show an explicit AAO recommendation for shorter follow-up intervals as a blanket rule for early glaucoma [N1-F1]. Instead, AAO guidance emphasizes **individualized monitoring** and more frequent follow-up after therapy changes or perioperative concerns [N1-F1][N1-R2]. That means the 6–12 month schedule is not wrong; it is the standard baseline for stable early glaucoma, but not the only possible schedule [N1-F1][N5-F4].

The standard current approach for early glaucoma is therefore:

- **Routine exams:** every 6–12 months for stable mild disease [N5-F4].
- **Monitoring tests:** visual field tests and optic nerve imaging, repeated as needed [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Adjustments:** frequency may vary based on patient risk factors and response to therapy [N1-R2].

So the physician’s advice is largely in line with current authoritative guidance, but it is **not a one-size-fits-all rule** [N1-F1][N5-F4].

---

## 2. When shorter intervals are appropriate

The evidence supports shorter intervals mainly when there is **evidence of progression, instability, or higher-risk factors** [N2-F2][N5-F4]. A direct study shows that clustered testing over 6 months detected a substantial proportion of eyes with rapid glaucoma progression, with high sensitivity for identifying fast progressors [N2-F2]. That means shorter, more frequent monitoring can be appropriate for patients whose disease may progress quickly, because conventional annual or semiannual testing may miss rapid change [N2-F2].

Other factors that support more frequent monitoring include:

- unstable disease or treatment response
- progressive optic nerve damage despite achieving target IOP
- higher-risk or less stable cases [N1-R2][N5-F4][N6-R4]

In practical terms, shorter intervals are not outdated; they are **appropriate when the patient is at higher risk of progression** [N2-F2][N5-F4].

---

## 3. How the physician’s intervals compare with current practice

The physician’s intervals are **mostly reasonable** as a starting point for early glaucoma [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The recommended schedule—routine exams every 6–12 months, visual field tests, and optic nerve imaging if progression is suspected—is consistent with current guidance [N1-F1][N5-F4]. However, they are **not outdated in the sense of being obsolete**; rather, they are the baseline schedule used when disease is stable [N5-F4].

The intervals are likely outdated **only when the patient has signs of progression, treatment instability, or other risk factors that make closer monitoring more appropriate** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. In that case, the schedule may need to be adjusted upward.

---

## 4. How to explain this to a patient in plain language

Here’s a simple way to put it:

- **If everything is stable:** every 6–12 months is a reasonable schedule [N5-F4].
- **If the disease is unstable, treatment is changing, or there are signs of progression:** more frequent visits are often needed [N1-R2][N2-F2].
- **If tests show change on visual fields or optic nerve imaging:** the doctor may check more often to be sure [N3-R3][N5-F4].
- **If the patient has thin corneas, low corneal hysteresis, or other risk factors:** they may need closer monitoring [N5-F4].

---

The physician’s intervals are **not outdated overall**. They are a solid, evidence-supported starting point for early glaucoma. But current guidance says follow-up should be individualized, which means shorter intervals may be appropriate when the patient is unstable, showing progression, or has other risk factors [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. In short: the intervals are a good baseline, but they are not the only possible schedule.
